planting.note: Set divisions or container plants in spring or early fall in full sun to light afternoon shade and lean, well-drained soil; avoid heavy clay that stays wet over winter.

directions: Colorwheel is a 2001 Saul Nurseries introduction prized for opening white and aging through soft lavender to deep purple, so a single clump carries several flower shades at once on the same branched stems. Grow in lean, sharply drained soil, since the fringed 3-inch blooms and evergreen basal rosette both suffer in soggy winter ground. Deadhead the spent heads through summer to keep fresh white buds opening and extend the color display into fall. Established clumps are drought- and deer-tolerant and benefit from division every three to four years to maintain vigorous bloom.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Omega Skyrocket Stokes' Aster (Giant Tall-Stemmed Selection)

planting.note: Start from seed indoors or set divisions in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; stake or grow among sturdy neighbors since the tall flower stalks can lean in open, windy sites.

directions: Omega Skyrocket was discovered by Atlanta Botanical Garden plantsmen near Omega, Georgia, and stands out as by far the tallest Stokes' aster in cultivation, sending 3 to 3.5-foot flower stalks up from a normal low evergreen rosette. The fluffy, cornflower-like blooms open 3 to 4 inches across in shades ranging from pale blue to whitish or purplish and make excellent, long-stemmed cut flowers. Because it is grown from seed, expect some variation in flower color between plants, and give it a bit more room and richer soil than compact cultivars to support the extra height. Peak bloom runs June into July with a lighter rebloom through September, especially if plants are deadheaded.

planting.note: Plant this patented (PP26164) selection from divisions or nursery starts in spring or early fall in full sun and moist, well-drained soil; the dusty blue-green foliage with a pale midvein is attractive even before bloom.

directions: Divinity is an Emerald Coast Growers introduction selected for its compact, tidy mound and pure white flowers that open with a faint yellow center blush before fading to clean white, holding well as cut flowers. The low, dense habit and dusty blue-green leaves make it useful at the front of a border without the flopping some taller white-flowered forms show. Keep soil evenly moist but well drained, since neither drought stress nor waterlogging suits the shallow root system, and deadhead regularly to sustain the long bloom season. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to renew vigor.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Set divisions or container plants in spring in full sun and lean, well-drained soil; good winter drainage is essential since wet feet in cold weather leads to crown rot.

directions: Wyoming produces fluffy, cornflower-like flowers 3 to 4 inches across in a saturated dark blue that reads noticeably deeper than the species and most powder-blue cultivars, held on upright, leafy stems to about a foot and a half tall. It combines well with silvery or chartreuse foliage plants that set off the intense flower color, and works equally well massed in a sunny border or cut for arrangements. Grow in lean, sharply drained soil and avoid heavy mulch against the crown, since rot rather than cold is the main threat to overwintering success. Deadhead through the June-to-fall bloom period to keep new buds forming.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Sow indoors or set divisions in spring in full sun to light shade and fertile, evenly moist but well-drained, slightly acid soil; this compact selection tolerates a bit more shade than most Stokes' aster cultivars.

directions: Träumerei was introduced by Jelitto Seeds in 1990 and forms a compact, upright rosette of leathery, softly spiny leaves topped by large, fringed flower heads that open white with a delicate pink blush, giving the blooms a dreamy, watercolor quality that matches the German name meaning reverie. It prefers richer, more evenly moist soil than most Stokes' aster selections, though it still needs good drainage to avoid crown rot over winter. Deadhead spent flower heads to encourage continued bud production from midsummer into autumn, and divide crowded clumps every few years in spring. The compact habit suits the front of a border or a container planting better than taller Stokesia cultivars.
